title: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH THE DEAD KING’S CONCUBINE—AND ONE QUESTION NEARLY SET A KINGDOM ON FIRE
paragraphs: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH THE DEAD KING’S CONCUBINE—AND ONE QUESTION NEARLY SET A KINGDOM ON FIRE

The scandal of Abner and Rizpah in 2 Samuel 3:7–11 reveals how wounded pride, political ambition, and an accusation that Scripture never confirms can turn loyalty into betrayal. But beneath the palace scandal lies a terrifying question: What happens when people care more about protecting their power than surrendering to the will of God?
He had fought for the king. He had defended the royal family. He had held a collapsing kingdom together.
Then came one accusation.
One woman’s name.
One question that sounded almost too dangerous to ask.
And suddenly, the man who had spent years defending Saul’s dynasty was preparing to help bring that dynasty down.
The woman was Rizpah.
The accused man was Abner.
The accuser was Ish-bosheth, Saul’s surviving son who had been made king over Israel.
And the accusation?
That Abner had slept with Rizpah, a concubine of the late King Saul.
But here is what makes this ancient scandal even more disturbing.
The Bible never actually tells us whether Abner did it.
Read that again.
A kingdom was shaken by an accusation whose truth the biblical narrator does not establish.
And before you decide this is simply another ugly story about ancient kings, ask yourself something.
Have you ever watched a relationship collapse because someone believed the worst before knowing the truth?
Have you ever been accused of something you didn't do?
Or, more painfully, have you ever been so angry at being questioned that your response became more destructive than the accusation itself?
Because this story is not only about what may have happened inside a royal household three thousand years ago.
It is about what happens inside the human heart when pride feels threatened.
And somewhere in this story, you may recognize a part of yourself you have spent years trying not to see.
The Bible introduces the accusation with chilling simplicity.
“Now Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ish-bosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7, KJV
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say Rizpah seduced Abner.
It does not say Abner forced himself upon Rizpah.
It does not say the accusation was proven.
It does not even tell us what Rizpah said.
Her name appears at the center of a political explosion, but her own voice is absent.
That silence matters.
Because sometimes the people whose lives are most affected by a scandal are the very people whose voices are never heard.
And Rizpah was not simply a nameless woman in a palace.
She was the daughter of Aiah.
She was a concubine of Saul, the former king.
She was a real person living in a royal household where women could become entangled in struggles for male authority and succession.
Scripture gives us no permission to invent her motives, her consent, or her personal involvement in the alleged encounter.
We must not turn her into a villain merely because powerful men argued over her.
And we must not pretend to know her private suffering when the text has not revealed it.
But we can recognize something deeply troubling.
Two men were fighting over authority, and a woman’s intimate life had become the center of their conflict.
How often does that still happen?
Someone’s reputation becomes ammunition.
Someone’s past becomes a weapon.
Someone’s name becomes a battlefield for people who are really fighting about something else.
And while everyone argues about who has power, the person caught in the middle can become almost invisible.
But to understand why Ish-bosheth’s question was so explosive, we need to understand what had already happened to Israel.
King Saul was dead.
Jonathan was dead.
The kingdom was fractured.
David had been anointed by God and was reigning over Judah from Hebron, while Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, had been established as king over the other Israelite tribes through Abner’s influence.
The nation was living through a painful struggle over the throne.
And Abner was no ordinary military officer.
He had been the commander of Saul’s army.
He possessed military influence, political connections, and the authority to strengthen or weaken Ish-bosheth’s rule.
In fact, 2 Samuel 3:6 tells us that Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.
That detail is not accidental.
It sets the stage for everything that follows.
Because Ish-bosheth wore the crown, but Abner possessed much of the power that helped sustain it.
And then Ish-bosheth asked whether Abner had gone in to his father’s concubine.
In the Hebrew text, the accusation includes the words:
בָּאתָ אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי
Ba’ta el-pilegesh avi.
Literally, “You went in to my father’s concubine.”
The expression “went in to” is a biblical idiom that, in this context, refers to sexual relations.
This was not an accusation that Abner had merely visited Rizpah.
It was an accusation of sexual involvement with a woman who had belonged to the deceased king’s household.
And in the political world of the ancient monarchy, access to a king’s wives or concubines could carry implications of royal power.
Later in 2 Samuel 16:21–22, Absalom publicly takes David’s concubines as part of his rebellion against his father.
In 1 Kings 2:13–25, Solomon interprets Adonijah’s request for Abishag as a threat connected to the kingdom.
Those passages do not prove that Abner was trying to seize Ish-bosheth’s throne.
They do, however, help explain why Ish-bosheth could have understood the alleged relationship as far more than a private sexual offense.
If Abner had taken a woman from Saul’s royal household, the act could have been perceived as a claim to authority associated with Saul himself.
That is why this question carried political danger.
And that is why Abner’s response was so explosive.
Scripture says:
“Then was Abner very wroth for the words of Ish-bosheth...” — 2 Samuel 3:8, KJV
Very angry.
Not mildly offended.
Not simply disappointed.
Furious.
Abner then responded with words that exposed how deeply the accusation had wounded his sense of honor.

“Am I a dog's head, which against Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father, to his brethren, and to his friends, and have not delivered thee into the hand of David, that thou chargest me to day with a fault concerning this woman?” — 2 Samuel 3:8, KJV
Can you hear the outrage?
After everything I have done for your family?
After everything I have protected?
After all the opportunities I have had to abandon you?
This is how you repay me?
Abner was reminding Ish-bosheth that he had defended Saul’s house rather than handing its interests over to David.
He saw the accusation as an insult to years of loyalty.
But notice something else.
Abner’s recorded response is a defense of his service and honor, not a clear account of what actually happened with Rizpah.
He does not provide evidence establishing his innocence.
Neither does the narrator provide evidence establishing his guilt.
The accusation remains unresolved in the passage.
That should make us careful.
Because the Bible sometimes tells us what people said without telling us that everything they said was true.
And spiritual maturity requires learning the difference.
A person’s anger does not prove innocence.
A person’s accusation does not prove guilt.
A person’s position does not make their words automatically trustworthy.
And a person's silence does not automatically mean they have something to hide.
Proverbs 18:17 says:
“He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.”
In other words, the first account may sound convincing until it is examined.
How many families could have been spared years of bitterness if they had remembered that?
How many friendships might still be alive?
How many churches might have avoided division?
How many reputations could have been protected?
We live in a world where accusations can travel faster than evidence.
One screenshot.
One rumor.
One edited conversation.
One story told by someone who is hurting.
And before the facts have been established, people begin choosing sides.
But followers of Jesus are not called to be careless with truth.
We are called to be truthful, just, and discerning.
That means refusing to conceal genuine wrongdoing.
It also means refusing to condemn someone merely because an allegation is dramatic.
Biblical justice does not demand that we ignore victims.
And biblical mercy does not demand that we abandon evidence.
Both truth and compassion matter to God.
But the story takes an even darker turn.
Abner’s anger did not end with a protest.
He made a decision that threatened to overturn the political order he had helped establish.

“So do God to Abner, and more also, except, as the LORD hath sworn to David, even so I do to him; To translate the kingdom from the house of Saul, and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beer-sheba.” — 2 Samuel 3:9–10, KJV
There it is.
The man who had defended Saul’s house now swore to help transfer the kingdom to David.
And here is the detail that should make every believer uncomfortable.
Abner invoked what the LORD had promised David.
He recognized David’s divinely appointed kingship.
Yet until this confrontation, he had continued strengthening Saul’s dynasty.
The text does not reveal everything Abner knew, believed, or intended before this moment.
But it does reveal that, in his anger, he appealed to God’s purpose for David.
And that raises a question that reaches beyond Abner.
How long can a person know what God has said while continuing to defend what God has not called them to preserve?
It is possible to recognize biblical truth and still resist its implications.
It is possible to speak about surrender while desperately protecting control.
It is possible to defend a ministry, a reputation, a relationship, or a position so fiercely that we forget who the true King is.
Sometimes our deepest spiritual struggle is not that we do not know what is right.
It is that doing what is right may cost us something we do not want to release.
A title.
An influence.
An advantage.
A relationship.
A secret.
A version of ourselves that other people admire.
And so we negotiate with conviction.
We delay obedience.
We convince ourselves that tomorrow will be a better time.
Until something exposes the instability of the kingdom we have been building inside our own hearts.
But we must be careful not to romanticize Abner’s decision.
The fact that his new political direction aligned with David’s promised kingship does not automatically make his anger righteous or his motives pure.
Scripture records his oath, but it does not pronounce every aspect of his conduct holy.
God’s purposes are not made righteous by the questionable motives of everyone involved in advancing them.
And this is one of the most sobering truths in the entire story.
You can move toward the right outcome for the wrong reason.
You can say something true because you want revenge.
You can defend justice because your pride has been wounded.
You can change sides not because you have repented, but because the people on your old side offended you.
You can even use the language of God’s will while your heart is still demanding personal vindication.
That is why following Jesus requires more than being on the side that eventually wins.
It requires surrendering our motives to Him.
Because Christ is not merely interested in where our feet are going.
He is concerned with what rules our hearts.
Then comes one of the most revealing sentences in the passage.
“And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him.” — 2 Samuel 3:11, KJV
Ish-bosheth was king.
But he was afraid.
The man who sat on the throne could not answer the man who held so much practical power.
The crown was on Ish-bosheth’s head.
Yet fear was in his heart.
And there is something painfully recognizable about that.
You can look successful and still be terrified.
You can hold a respected position and still feel powerless.
You can have people calling you a leader while privately knowing that you are controlled by the approval, anger, or influence of someone else.
You can smile in public while living under the pressure of losing everything.
And sometimes, the things we call security are merely the things we are most afraid to lose.
A position cannot give you peace.
Influence cannot cleanse your conscience.
Public approval cannot heal your soul.
And power cannot save you from the truth.
Only God can give the kind of security that does not collapse when the room turns against you.
But now we need to return to the person whose name began this confrontation.
Rizpah.
Because the Bible does not leave her story in 2 Samuel 3.
Years later, in 2 Samuel 21, she appears again in one of the most heartbreaking scenes in the historical books of Scripture.
Two of her sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, were among seven descendants of Saul handed over to the Gibeonites during David’s reign in connection with Saul’s bloodguilt against them.
The men were executed.
And Rizpah did something that makes her unforgettable.
She spread sackcloth upon a rock and remained near the exposed bodies, keeping birds away by day and wild animals away by night, until rain fell upon them from heaven.
The text does not give us a complete account of her thoughts.
It does not record a speech from her.
But it records her vigil.
A mother staying near the bodies of her sons.
A woman whose name had once been caught in a royal accusation now standing in the shadow of devastating loss.
And when David learned what Rizpah had done, he arranged for the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and the executed descendants to be gathered and buried in the family tomb.
The passage then says that God responded to supplication for the land.
Rizpah’s vigil is not presented as a declaration that she was sinless, nor does it settle the earlier accusation involving Abner.
But it does force us to see her as more than a political detail.
She was a mother.
She suffered.
And her actions became part of a story the king could no longer ignore.
Isn't it remarkable how easily people can be reduced to a scandal when we do not take time to see their humanity?
We remember the accusation.
We debate the men.
We analyze the politics.
But we may forget the woman whose name was attached to it all.
There is a lesson here for every believer who has ever repeated a story about someone without considering the person behind the story.
That person has a life beyond the accusation.
A family.
A history.
Wounds you may not know.
And a soul that matters to God.
James 3 warns us about the destructive power of the tongue.
Words can set entire lives ablaze.
And while James is not commenting specifically on Abner and Rizpah, the principle reaches straight into this story.
Our words are never as small as we pretend they are.
They can expose truth.
They can protect the vulnerable.
They can call sinners to repentance.
But they can also humiliate, manipulate, deceive, and destroy.
This is why the Gospel calls us to something radically different from the way the world handles scandal.
Not denial.
Not gossip disguised as concern.
Not automatic condemnation.
Not defending powerful people at the expense of the wounded.
But truth spoken in love.
Justice pursued without favoritism.
Repentance where sin has occurred.
Mercy where mercy is needed.
And humility where we do not possess all the facts.
Yet there is an even greater contrast in this story.
Abner and Ish-bosheth were fighting over the security of a fragile earthly kingdom.
But centuries later, another King would come.
A King whose authority would not depend on military commanders.
A King who would not need to seize another man's household to establish His throne.
A King who would not protect His glory by crushing the weak.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And unlike the kings and commanders of Israel’s divided monarchy, Jesus came not to defend a threatened earthly dynasty, but to fulfill God’s saving purpose.
He came as the promised Son of David.
The true King.
The righteous Judge.
The Savior of sinners.
In Luke 1:32–33, the angel announced that God would give Jesus the throne of His father David and that His kingdom would have no end.
Think about the contrast.
Abner threatened to transfer a kingdom because his honor had been challenged.
Jesus willingly endured dishonor to bring sinners into His kingdom.
Abner was furious at an accusation.
Jesus was falsely accused, mocked, and condemned, yet entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly.
Abner’s story unfolded amid a struggle for political control.
Jesus declared that His kingdom was not of this world.
And when Christ stood before His accusers, He did not need to manipulate a military alliance to prove His authority.
He went to the cross.
Not because He was powerless.
But because He came to save.
Isaiah 53:7 describes the suffering Servant:
“He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter...”
And 1 Peter 2:23 tells us that when Jesus suffered, He did not threaten in return, but entrusted Himself to the righteous Judge.
Do you see the difference?
Human pride says, You will regret humiliating me.
Jesus showed a righteousness that did not depend on revenge.
Human ambition says, I must protect my throne.
Jesus, though truly King, humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
Human sin says, I will make you pay for what you did.
The Gospel declares that Christ bore the judgment sinners could never bear for themselves.
And this is where the story stops being merely an ancient political scandal.
Because the greatest crisis in your life may not be what someone accused you of doing.
It may be what is actually happening between your soul and God.
You may have been misunderstood.
You may have been betrayed.
You may have been treated unfairly.
Those wounds matter.
But even if every accusation against you were false, you would still need the grace of Jesus Christ.
And even if some accusations against you were true, you would not be beyond the reach of His forgiveness.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends sin does not matter.
But that God is so holy that sin must be judged, and so merciful that He sent His Son to save sinners.
The cross does not make evil harmless.
It reveals how serious evil truly is.
And it reveals how far God's love went to redeem those who could never rescue themselves.
Listen to the words of Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we cleaned up every secret.
Not after we learned to sound spiritual.
Not after everyone finally believed our side of the story.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And the Greek New Testament gives us a beautiful expression of what that grace produces in a redeemed life.
In 2 Corinthians 5:17, Paul writes:
καινὴ κτίσις
Kainē ktisis.
“A new creation.”
The surrounding verse declares that if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old has passed away, and the new has come.
The expression does not mean your past never happened.
It does not mean consequences disappear.
It does not mean everyone you hurt must immediately trust you again.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored in this life.
It means that through union with Christ, a new reality has begun.
Your sin does not have to remain your master.
Your shame does not have to become your identity.
Your past does not have to determine the direction of your eternity.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Repentance is possible.
Transformation is not merely a religious slogan.
It is the work of God’s grace.
But grace is not permission to continue in sin.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners calls them to repentance.
And repentance is more than feeling bad because you were exposed.
The Greek word commonly used in the New Testament is:
μετάνοια
Metanoia.
Repentance—a change of mind and heart that turns a person toward God and bears fruit in a changed life.
It is not simply embarrassment.
It is not public damage control.
It is not crying because your reputation has suffered.
It is turning away from sin and toward the Lord.
And perhaps that is where this story finds you today.
Maybe you are like Ish-bosheth, terrified of losing control.
Maybe you are like Abner, carrying an anger that has begun to govern your decisions.
Maybe you have been treated like Rizpah, discussed by people who never stopped to consider your humanity.
Maybe you have been falsely accused.
Or maybe you have been the one who made an accusation without first seeking the truth.
Maybe your pride has destroyed relationships you once prayed God would protect.
Maybe you know the right Scriptures, but there is still an area of your life where you resist the authority of Christ.
You don't need to manufacture a dramatic confession for strangers.
But you do need to be truthful before God.
Because the Lord already knows what you are afraid to admit.
He knows the anger beneath your silence.
He knows the bitterness beneath your politeness.
He knows the compromises behind your public image.
He knows the nights when you lie awake replaying conversations, wishing you had said something different.
He knows what was done to you.
And He knows what you have done.
Yet the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Not to protect a false version of yourself.
Not to bargain for a better reputation.
Not to pretend that your wounds or your sins are insignificant.
Come because Jesus is the Savior who died and rose again.
Come because His mercy is greater than the shame you cannot undo.
Come because His truth can expose what is hidden without leaving a repentant sinner without hope.
Come because you cannot crown Jesus as Lord while insisting that your pride remain king.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because something in these words has reached a place you normally keep hidden, do not mistake conviction for rejection.
The Holy Spirit's work of conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is a summons to turn toward the Savior.
You can pray, right where you are:

“Lord Jesus, You know the truth about me. You know where I have been wounded, and You know where I have sinned. Forgive my pride, my bitterness, my careless words, and my resistance to Your will. Teach me to love truth more than my reputation, holiness more than my comfort, and You more than my need to control everything. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects what your heart is struggling to express, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Not to impress anyone.
Not because writing a comment earns forgiveness.
But because sometimes a simple, honest declaration can become the beginning of a conversation about the grace we desperately need.
You do not owe the internet the private details of your wounds. You can be honest without exposing everything.

And if God has already brought you through a season of false accusation, painful repentance, or unexpected restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone else may need to know that Christ's grace can sustain a person through circumstances that once seemed unbearable.
Because the Church should not be a place where wounded people are turned into entertainment.
It should be a people who speak truth, practice justice, bear one another's burdens, and point sinners to Jesus.
And that brings me to something close to the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Scandal spreads easily.
Outrage spreads quickly.
But biblical truth often requires something the modern world is losing.
Patience.
Attention.
Humility.
A willingness to read beyond the headline.
A willingness to let Scripture correct us rather than using Scripture merely to defend what we already believe.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
To keep bringing the Word of God into the places where people are hurting, questioning, struggling, repenting, and searching for hope.
Not to build a kingdom around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell the grace of God.
But to point people back to Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship.
A single share may introduce someone to Scripture who would never have searched for this passage on their own.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have drifted from faith, and those who are still exploring who Jesus really is.
Not because a page can save anyone.
Only Christ can do that.
But because faithful teaching can direct people to the Savior.

It is a voluntary act of support that can help sustain the time, work, resources, and continuing effort required to create and share Scripture-centered teaching, develop discipleship materials, and expand the reach of Gospel Warrior.
For those who prayerfully choose to give from the resources God has entrusted to them, that support can be an expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
But I want to be biblically clear about something important.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your salvation is not for sale.
Your access to Jesus is not behind a paywall.
And no one should feel spiritually inferior because they cannot afford to give.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and spiritual growth more accessible.
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation.
The greater purpose remains the same: helping people grow in biblical understanding, prayer, repentance, faith, and obedience to Christ.
You can help by tagging someone who needs encouragement.
You can help by returning to the Scriptures, testing what you read, and letting God's Word shape your life.
Because the mission is not to gather people around Gospel Warrior as though a ministry were the source of life.
The mission is to keep pointing people to the One who is.
Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that royal confrontation.
Ish-bosheth asked a question.
Abner became furious.
A political alliance began to unravel.
A woman’s name stood at the center of a dispute whose underlying allegation Scripture never resolves.
And an already divided kingdom moved closer to a change in power.
The next verses show Abner seeking an agreement with David, and the broader chapter eventually records Abner's murder by Joab.
Abner would not live to see David's rule fully established over all Israel.
His political influence was real.
His anger was real.
His plans were real.
But his life was still fragile.
And so was the power everyone was fighting to possess.
That is the tragedy of building your identity around a throne you cannot keep.
You can spend your life defending your importance, only to discover that your importance could never save you.
You can win arguments and lose relationships.
You can preserve appearances and lose integrity.
You can gain influence while your soul grows increasingly distant from God.
But there is another way.
The way of Jesus.
The way of truth without cruelty.
Repentance without excuses.
Humility without pretending.
Grace without compromise.
Forgiveness without denying justice.
And a life surrendered to a King whose kingdom will never fall.
What am I defending so fiercely that I have stopped asking whether Jesus wants me to surrender it?
Is it your pride?
Your anger?
Your need to be believed?
Your desire to win?
Your fear of losing control?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your unwillingness to repent?
Bring it to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when everyone finally understands your side.
Not when your life looks respectable enough to approach Him.
Today.
Because the most important throne in your life is not the one other people think you occupy.
It is the one your heart has given its allegiance to.
And if Jesus is truly your King, then even your deepest scandal does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
The cross declares that sin is serious.
The empty tomb declares that death has been defeated.
And the Gospel declares that all who turn to Christ in faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
Share if someone you love needs this truth.
But whatever you decide, never forget this:
The kingdom you build around your pride will eventually crumble, but the life you surrender to Jesus rests in the hands of a King whose grace can outlast your darkest chapter.
